# zero-auth

zero-auth is a small TypeScript authentication layer for Node.js and Express
APIs. It provides JWT access tokens, refresh-token rotation, HTTP-only cookies,
signed double-submit CSRF protection, optional authentication, and role and
permission authorization. It does not provide a hosted user database,
password hashing, OAuth providers, MFA, or a user-management interface.

## Start here

Install the package with:

~~~bash
npm install @0-auth/zero-auth express
~~~

Create an auth instance with separate secrets of at least 32 characters:

~~~ts
import { createAuth } from "@0-auth/zero-auth";

const auth = createAuth({
  accessSecret: process.env.JWT_ACCESS_SECRET!,
  refreshSecret: process.env.JWT_REFRESH_SECRET!,
});
~~~

Optional JWT policy:

~~~ts
const auth = createAuth({
  accessSecret: process.env.JWT_ACCESS_SECRET!,
  refreshSecret: process.env.JWT_REFRESH_SECRET!,
  jwt: {
    issuer: "https://api.example.com",
    audience: "web-app",
    clockTolerance: 5,
  },
});
~~~

The configured issuer and audience are written to new tokens and enforced on
access and refresh verification. Clock tolerance is measured in seconds.

Protect an Express route:

~~~ts
app.get("/profile", auth.protect(), (req, res) => {
  res.json({ user: req.user });
});

app.use(auth.errorHandler);
~~~

## Authentication choices

- Bearer tokens are explicit headers for mobile, CLI, and server-to-server clients.
- HTTP-only cookies keep browser token values away from JavaScript.
- Cookie-authenticated state-changing requests require CSRF protection.
- Access tokens should be short-lived, usually about 15 minutes.
- Refresh tokens should use rotation and a shared atomic store when replay
  detection or multiple instances matter.

## Authorization

Run protect before authorization:

~~~ts
app.patch(
  "/users/:id",
  auth.protect(),
  auth.authorize(["admin", "support"]),
  auth.authorizePermissions(["users:update"]),
  updateUserHandler,
);
~~~

authorize allows any matching role. authorizePermissions requires every listed
permission from the verified JWT permissions claim. Resource ownership remains
an application responsibility.

## Cookie CSRF protection

~~~ts
app.use(auth.csrf());

app.get("/auth/csrf-token", (_req, res) => {
  res.json({ csrfToken: auth.csrfToken(res) });
});
~~~

By default, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE requests carrying an auth cookie need
the same signed value in the readable CSRF cookie and configured request
header. Missing or invalid values return 403 AUTH_CSRF_INVALID.

## Refresh rotation

When rotate is true, consumeRefreshToken must atomically mark the incoming jti
and return true only for the first request. Redis SET NX or a database
constraint can provide this guarantee. registerRefreshToken tracks replacement
tokens, and onRefreshReuse can revoke the token family.

Alternatively, pass a refreshStore with consume(jti, context), optional
register(jti, context), and optional revokeFamily(familyId). The package wires
these methods into the rotation lifecycle automatically; consume must be atomic.
For ioredis-compatible clients, createRedisRevocationStore(redis, ttlSeconds?)
provides this store without bundling a Redis client dependency. It marks a
compromised family before member revocation and atomically rejects late
replacement registration.

The legacy isRevoked and revokeRefreshToken hooks remain supported with a
warning, but their separate check/write sequence is not concurrency-safe.

## Errors

The package returns structured AuthError responses:

- 401 AUTH_TOKEN_MISSING
- 401 AUTH_TOKEN_INVALID
- 401 AUTH_TOKEN_EXPIRED
- 401 AUTH_UNAUTHORIZED
- 403 AUTH_FORBIDDEN
- 403 AUTH_CSRF_INVALID

Use the exact error code for client behavior rather than matching message text.

## Deployment

Your application owns secrets, users, password hashing, TLS, CORS, rate
limiting, storage, monitoring, and resource ownership. Use HTTPS, separate
high-entropy secrets, secure cookie settings, a trusted proxy configuration,
and a shared refresh store for horizontally scaled deployments.
